First Day of School

A personalized story for starting school: your child lives their first day of first grade as the hero — and walks in with confidence instead of butterflies.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

The school bag has been standing ready for weeks and the pencil case is packed — yet at dinner, out of nowhere: “What if I don't know where to sit?” Many parents experience the summer before the first day of school as an emotional seesaw: the same child who proudly tells everyone about starting first grade lies awake longer than usual at night. Both belong together — excitement and a nervous tummy are not opposites.

After two years of kindergarten, your child was one of the big kids there — starting school makes them the youngest all over again. On top of that come brand-new expectations: sitting still, finishing tasks, keeping track of their own snack and gym bag. At six or seven, children can picture the future well enough to worry about it, but they lack the lived experience that tells them they can handle transitions. That gap is what makes starting school emotionally demanding, even for children who can hardly wait.

A story can help fill that gap. First, it creates distance: your child watches the hero from the outside and can think about the first day of school without being in the middle of it. When that hero wears their own face, something else happens: “If story-me can do this, so can I.” And third, the big day gets a mental dress rehearsal — the walk to school, the classroom, the teacher, the break in the playground. What a child has rehearsed inside feels far less foreign on the real morning.

In the personalized back-to-school story, your child lives that exact day as the main character: school bag on their back, stepping into the classroom, finding their seat, joining the first game at break time. The plot takes the nervousness seriously and moves gently from a wobbly morning to a proud afternoon — no lecturing, just familiar situations and your child's face on every page. You can try the first story for free.

The book works best if you read it for the first time two to three weeks before school starts in mid-August — and then again and again. Let your child retell the story in their own words; it shows you what is really on their mind. Walk the actual route to school and compare it with the book. If the first week gets bumpy, go back to the pages where the hero manages. And if intense fear lasts for weeks or your child keeps complaining of stomach aches, talk to the teacher — a story supports, but it does not replace professional advice.

What your child learns

Confidence in transitions, independence in daily school life, coping with new situations, asking for help, building positive anticipation

Recommended age

5-7 years

Frequently Asked Questions

How can I prepare my child for starting school?

Talk through the day in concrete terms: when it starts, what happens in the morning, who picks them up. Walk the route to school together a few times and let your child practise the things they will need to do alone — packing the school bag, zipping the jacket, opening the snack box. Just as important: keep your own nerves out of it and talk about school as something your child can handle.

What if my child is afraid of school?

Take the fear seriously instead of brushing it off with a quick “you'll be fine”. Ask what exactly worries them — often it is something concrete and solvable, like not finding the way or not knowing anyone. Most fears settle during the first weeks of school; if they persist, talk to the teacher early.

My child loved kindergarten — why are they still nervous about first grade?

In kindergarten your child was one of the oldest and knew every rule — at school everything is new and they are the youngest again. This nervousness is not a step backwards; it shows your child understands how meaningful the change is. It usually fades as soon as the new routine becomes familiar.

When should we start talking about the first day of school?

Answer questions whenever they come up — but don't build up tension for months. Two to three weeks before the first day is a good moment to get concrete: walk the route, lay out the materials, read stories about starting school. That keeps the preparation close enough to the event to actually carry.

From what age does a personalized back-to-school story make sense?

It helps most in the year before and around the start of school, roughly ages five to seven. At that age a child follows the plot, recognises themselves as the main character and can connect the story to their own first day.
